name: Abomination
caseNote: Subject is a former KGB agent who deliberately exposed himself to gamma radiation and became a scaly creature stronger than the Hulk. Retains his full intellect in that form. Agents should not comment on his appearance.
notes: Infobox teams (A.I.M., Masters of Evil, Lethal Legion, Thunderbolts) are adversarial, adaptation-only or single-storyline links, so none are kept.

name: Absorbing Man
caseNote: Subject, a former boxer, can take on the properties of anything he touches after drinking a potion prepared by Loki. Longtime partner of Titania. Handshakes are discouraged.
notes: Wikipedia lists his species as human mutate, but his powers come from Loki's magic potion (magic). Reformed into an antihero in recent years after decades as a villain; his live-action role in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. does not count.

name: Agent Venom
caseNote: Subject is Flash Thompson, Peter Parker's high-school bully turned friend, who lost both legs in the Iraq War. Bonded with the Venom symbiote under a military program, which let him walk again. Bonding sessions are limited to 48 hours; Subject is asked to keep track.
notes: Debut uses Flash Thompson's first appearance; he first became Agent Venom in ASM #654 (April 2011). MCU is true because Flash Thompson (Tony Revolori) appears from Homecoming onward, though never as Agent Venom.

name: Aleta Ogord
caseNote: Subject is an Arcturan who for years shared a single body with her adoptive brother Stakar as Starhawk. Now projects solid-light constructs in her own right. Agents are advised not to raise the topic of sibling rivalry.
notes: Arcturan by birth, but her light powers came from merging with Stakar through the Hawk God, so origin is set to cosmic (alien is arguable). The aliases Starhawk, Stakar and One Who Knows are left out as Starhawk's; Ravagers is MCU-only.

name: Alex Power
caseNote: Subject, eldest of the four Power siblings, received gravity control from a dying Kymellian and became a founding member of Power Pack. He later joined Reed Richards' Future Foundation. Curfew enforcement is outside this office's remit.
notes: His powers were handed over by Whitey, a dying Kymellian alien, so alien is the closest fit even though Alex is human (cosmic is arguable). 'Alex Power' redirects to the Power Pack article, and his brief 1994 New Warriors stint as Powerpax is left out.

name: Alex Wilder
caseNote: Subject was the founding leader and strategist of the Runaways until he was exposed as the Pride's mole. He has no superpowers, only a talent for planning. References from former teammates are unavailable.
notes: He was introduced as the Runaways' leader and then revealed as the Pride's mole, and his later appearances (Young Masters, Power Man and Iron Fist) are villainous; Wikipedia files him as both hero and villain. Rhenzy Feliz played him in Hulu's Runaways, which does not count toward mcu.

name: Amadeus Cho
caseNote: Subject is a teenage super-genius who later used nanobots to absorb the Hulk's gamma radiation into himself. Has served with the Champions and led the Agents of Atlas in the field. Agents should assume he has already done the math.
notes: Wikipedia gives January 2005, but Amazing Fantasy vol. 2 #15 went on sale November 30, 2005 with a January 2006 cover date. Origin is mutate for his gamma-powered Hulk/Brawn identity; he was an unpowered genius before 2015, and a planned live-action debut was cut from Brave New World.

name: America Chavez
mcuFirst: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
caseNote: Subject punches star-shaped portals between realities and has served with the Young Avengers, the Ultimates and the West Coast Avengers. She also possesses superhuman strength and flight. Do not expect her to use the door.
notes: She was originally an alien from the Utopian Parallel; a 2021 retcon made her a human whose powers came from experiments with extra-dimensional energy, so origin is mutate (Wikipedia lists both). Thunderbolts, Defenders and Champions appear only in the infobox and are left out.

name: Anole
caseNote: Subject is a reptilian mutant with camouflage, wall-crawling and regenerative abilities who trained at the Xavier Institute. On Krakoa he co-owned a tiki bar with the Blob. Surveillance is hampered by his camouflage.
notes: His teams were Xavier Institute student squads with no TEAMS id, and he never served on an X-Men main roster, so primaryTeam is none.

name: Ant-Man (Hank Pym)
caseNote: Subject is a biochemist who discovered the size-altering Pym particles. Founding Avenger who has operated as Ant-Man, Giant-Man, Goliath and Yellowjacket. Also built Ultron, a matter still under review.
notes: Origin contested: Wikipedia lists him as a human mutate whose size powers came from his own ingested Pym-particle formulas, while the MCU version relies on a suit (tech).

name: Ant-Man (Scott Lang)
caseNote: Subject is a reformed thief and electronics expert who stole the Ant-Man suit to save his daughter's life. Shrinks to insect size and commands ants via a cybernetic helmet. Agents should check their pockets after meetings.
notes: 'Giant-Man' left out of aliases because it belongs primarily to Hank Pym in the comics.

name: Archangel
caseNote: Subject is a founding X-Man who flies on feathered wings, once replaced with razor-edged metal wings by Apocalypse. Heir to the Worthington fortune and a longtime financier of mutant teams. Agents are advised to watch for falling feathers.
notes: He debuted as and is widely known as Angel, so 'Angel' is kept as an alias even though the list also has The Angel (Thomas Halloway). 'Death' (his Horseman name) is omitted because it belongs to the cosmic entity Death.

name: Ares
caseNote: Subject is the Olympian god of war and son of Zeus. Long a foe of Hercules and Thor, he later served with the Mighty Avengers and the Dark Avengers. Subject has also worked as a carpenter.
notes: A villain for most of his history but recast as an antihero from 2006 to 2010 (Mighty Avengers, Dark Avengers); Wikipedia flags him as both hero and villain.

name: Arishem
caseNote: Subject is a Celestial empowered to judge which civilizations live and which die. Has led every Celestial Host to visit Earth. Agents are advised to remain worthy for fifty years at a time.
notes: Counts as MCU because he appears on screen in Eternals as a CGI Celestial voiced by David Kaye. Alignment is contested: the comics present an impartial judge, but he is usually grouped with the Eternals' antagonists.

name: Arnim Zola
caseNote: Subject is a Swiss biochemist who now inhabits an android body, his face displayed on a screen in its chest. A longtime Hydra scientist and associate of the Red Skull. Agents should not attempt to change the channel.
notes: Origin set to synthetic because he has lived in android bodies since his 1977 debut; Wikipedia calls him a 'human mutate-cyborg', and the MCU version is human before becoming a computer-stored mind.

name: Aurora
caseNote: Subject flies at superhuman speed and generates brilliant light, classically by joining hands with her twin brother, Northstar. Raised apart from him at a strict religious school in Quebec; founding member of Alpha Flight. Agents are advised not to separate the twins.
notes: Her brief X-Men stint and her mind-controlled Weapon X service are left out of teams as not notable tenures.

name: Ayesha
caseNote: Subject is a golden-skinned being engineered by the Enclave after their earlier creation, Him. Has operated as Paragon, Her and Kismet. Agents are advised not to steal from Subject's people.
notes: Wikipedia covers her as Kismet and its infobox marks her as a hero, but the MCU Ayesha (Elizabeth Debicki) is a villain and her early comics roles were antagonistic, so alignment is contested. Origin: created by the Enclave (mutate); the MCU version is a Sovereign.

name: Balder
caseNote: Subject is an Asgardian prince, half-brother of Thor and a former King of Asgard. Once killed by a mistletoe arrow before Odin averted Ragnarok and later restored him. Mistletoe is prohibited at all Subject's functions.

name: Banshee
caseNote: Subject emits sonic screams powerful enough to carry him in flight. A former Interpol officer who joined the X-Men in 1975 and later co-ran the Generation X academy. Agents are advised to bring earplugs.
notes: He debuted as a coerced Factor Three operative before turning hero. Caleb Landry Jones's X-Men: First Class role is Fox, not MCU.

name: Baron Strucker
debutIssue: Sgt. Fury and His Howling Commandos #5
caseNote: Subject is a German aristocrat and former Nazi officer, founder and supreme leader of Hydra. Wears the Satan Claw, a gauntlet that amplifies his strength and delivers electric shocks. Hail with caution.
notes: Origin set to trained because he is defined by skill and command, though Wikipedia lists superhuman traits from the Satan Claw gauntlet and the Death Spore virus.

name: Baron Zemo
caseNote: Subject is the thirteenth holder of a German noble title and a persistent enemy of Captain America and the Avengers. Once disguised a team of villains as heroes and named them the Thunderbolts. The purple mask stays on.
notes: Record follows Helmut Zemo, the MCU's Zemo, who debuted as the Phoenix in 1973 and first appeared as Baron Zemo in 1982. The original Baron, his father Heinrich, debuted in The Avengers #4 (March 1964, flashback cameo), so the debut is contested.

name: Batroc the Leaper
caseNote: Subject is a French mercenary and master of savate, a form of kickboxing. Has clashed with Captain America for decades and occasionally leads a brigade of his own. Agents are advised to watch his feet.
notes: Wikipedia also lists the Thunderbolts and Masters of Evil, but his Thunderbolts stints were a forced draft and a King in Black tie-in, so only Batroc's Brigade is kept.

name: Beast
caseNote: Subject is a genius biochemist with the strength and agility of a great ape and a coat of blue fur. Founding X-Man who has also served with the Avengers and the Defenders. Agents are advised to bring a dictionary.
notes: Kelsey Grammer appears as an alternate-universe Beast in the mid-credits scene of The Marvels (2023). Born a mutant; the blue fur came later from a self-administered serum.

name: Beetle (Abner Jenkins)
caseNote: Subject is a former aircraft mechanic who built a winged suit of beetle-themed armor and turned to crime. Later reformed as MACH-1 of the Thunderbolts and ran security at the Raft. Agents are advised his armor upgrades are numbered.
notes: Alignment is contested: he was a villain as the Beetle from 1964 until the Thunderbolts debuted in 1997, then a reformed hero as MACH-1 and later MACH identities, so he is set to antihero as a character defined by switching sides. His Wikipedia page has no infobox, so the debut comes from its text.

name: Beyonder
caseNote: Subject is a near-omnipotent being from beyond the multiverse who built Battleworld for the original Secret Wars. Later visited Earth to study humanity and turned a building into solid gold. Agents should not explain money to Subject.
notes: The debut is a cameo (full appearance Secret Wars II). He is written mainly as male, but Wikipedia also files him as genderfluid (female form as Kosmos), and his origin has been retconned several times (Cosmic Cube, Inhuman-mutant hybrid, child of the Beyonders).

name: Big Wheel
caseNote: Subject is a businessman who embezzled from his own company and had the Tinkerer build him a giant armed wheel. Has since spoken at Vil-Anon meetings. Agents are advised to approach from the side.
notes: The infobox gives only 'The Amazing Spider-Man #183 (1978)'; that issue's cover date is August 1978.

name: Bishop
caseNote: Subject absorbs energy directed at him and redirects it as blasts. A mutant police officer from a dystopian future, branded with an M over his right eye. Agents are advised not to open fire.
notes: He was an antagonist hunting Hope Summers in the Messiah Complex era but is classified hero overall. Omar Sy's role is in Fox's Days of Future Past, not the MCU.

name: Black Cat
caseNote: Subject is a cat burglar who has alternated between adversary, ally and romantic interest of Spider-Man. Has Olympic-level acrobatic skill and has at times possessed the power to cause bad luck. Valuables in her vicinity should be considered already missing.
notes: Origin is contested: she began without powers, later gained psionic 'bad luck' powers from a Kingpin-backed experiment, and has gained and lost powers several times; trained reflects her core skills. The infobox also lists Avengers, A-Force and Defenders, which the article text does not support, so only Heroes for Hire (joined during Civil War) is counted.

name: Black Dwarf
caseNote: Subject is the Black Order's resident powerhouse. Was expelled from the Order after failing to take Wakanda, and was later killed by Ronan the Accuser. Known on some screens as Cull Obsidian.
notes: The debut is a one-panel cameo (full appearance Infinity #1, Oct 2013). In the MCU he is renamed Cull Obsidian (Terry Notary).

name: Black Knight (Dane Whitman)
caseNote: Subject is a physicist who took up the Black Knight mantle to redeem the name after his villainous uncle. Wields the cursed Ebony Blade and has served with the Avengers and the Defenders. Unauthorized personnel should not handle the sword.
notes: Origin contested: he has no innate powers and relies on the mystical Ebony Blade plus training (classed magic).

name: Black Panther
caseNote: Subject has ruled the technologically advanced African nation of Wakanda. Draws enhanced abilities from the sacred heart-shaped herb and wears a vibranium suit. Diplomatic immunity is presumed.
notes: Origin contested: his enhanced abilities come from the heart-shaped herb ritual tied to the Panther God Bast (classed magic), but he also relies on vibranium technology and training.

name: Black Widow
caseNote: Subject is a former Soviet spy trained in the Red Room who defected to the West. Longtime Avenger and S.H.I.E.L.D. operative with no superhuman powers. Her file should be presumed incomplete.
notes: Wikipedia notes Red Room biochemical augmentation slowed her aging but states she has no superhuman powers, so she is classed as trained.

name: Boomerang
caseNote: Subject is an Australian-born former major-league pitcher, banned for taking bribes. Throws trick boomerangs and once led a five-member Sinister Six. Agents are advised that he always comes back.
notes: Wikipedia merged his article into 'List of Marvel Comics characters: B' in 2024, so the debut comes from the infobox of its last full revision. He uses the name Comeback in 2026 comics; Sinister Six is set as his primary team because he led it in The Superior Foes of Spider-Man.

name: Cable
caseNote: Subject is the time-displaced son of Cyclops, raised in a distant future and partly overtaken by a techno-organic virus. Turned the New Mutants into X-Force. Agents are advised to count his pouches before engaging.
notes: The infobox lists Uncanny X-Men #201 (Jan 1986) for infant Nathan and New Mutants #87 (Mar 1990) for Cable, who was only later revealed to be the grown Nathan, so the debut is contested. Antihero is a judgment call for the militant soldier, and Josh Brolin's Deadpool 2 role is Fox, not MCU.

name: Calypso
caseNote: Subject is a voodoo priestess and the occasional lover and partner of Kraven the Hunter. Has used drums, potions and charms to hold the Lizard under her control. Agents are advised to decline any beverages.
notes: The infobox gives the name Calypso Ezili, though the article text calls her a nameless priestess. Her only live-action role is in Sony's Kraven the Hunter, which does not count.

name: Captain America
caseNote: Subject, a frail Army volunteer, was made peak human by the Super-Soldier Serum during World War II. Spent decades frozen in ice before leading the Avengers. Agents are reminded that the shield is not a frisbee.
notes: Infobox lists the December 20, 1940 on-sale date; the March 1941 cover date is used per rubric.

name: Captain Marvel (Carol Danvers)
caseNote: Subject is a former U.S. Air Force officer who gained Kree-derived powers when an alien device exploded. Previously operated as Ms. Marvel, Binary and Warbird. Absorbs energy; tasers are not recommended.
notes: Powers came from the Psyche-Magnitron explosion (mutate); a 2018 story added a Kree mother, so Wikipedia lists her as a human mutate/Kree hybrid. 'Ms. Marvel' left out of aliases because the game assigns it to Kamala Khan.

name: Cardiac
caseNote: Subject is Dr. Elias Wirtham, a surgeon whose heart was replaced with a beta-particle reactor. Operates as a vigilante, a practice that has put him at odds with Spider-Man. Agents are advised his pulse is unusual.
notes: Alignment is a judgment call: he is a vigilante first depicted as an enemy of Spider-Man, so he is set to antihero. The debut is his first appearance as Elias Wirtham; he first appeared as Cardiac in ASM #344 (February 1991).

name: Carnage
caseNote: Subject is serial killer Cletus Kasady, who bonded with an offspring of the Venom symbiote while sharing a prison cell with Eddie Brock. Regarded as Venom's archenemy. Cellmate assignments have since been reviewed.
notes: The Carnage article lists an unnamed appearance in ASM #345 (March 1991); Cletus Kasady's own article gives ASM #344, and he first appeared as Carnage in ASM #360-361 (1992). His live-action films are Sony's, not MCU.

name: Chameleon
caseNote: Subject is Dmitri Smerdyakov, a master of disguise who debuted in the first issue of The Amazing Spider-Man in 1963. Half-brother of Kraven the Hunter. Agents should verify the identity of everyone present at this briefing.
notes: MCU status rests on Wikipedia identifying Numan Acar's 'Dimitri' in Far From Home as Dmitri Smerdyakov; he never appears as the Chameleon there. Origin is contested: masks and gadgets at first, later a serum that made his features malleable (Wikipedia: human mutate).

name: Champion of the Universe
caseNote: Subject is an Elder of the Universe who channels the Power Primordial entirely into physical might. Travels the cosmos challenging the strongest fighters he can find. Agents are advised to decline all rematches.
notes: Wikipedia says he is 'not necessarily a villain' but has played the role, and files him as a supervillain, so alignment is somewhat contested.

name: Charlie-27
caseNote: Subject is a Jovian militia captain descended from colonists engineered for Jupiter's gravity, with eleven times a normal human's muscle mass. Founding member of the original Guardians of the Galaxy. Agents are advised against arm-wrestling.
notes: Jovians are genetically engineered descendants of human colonists, classed as alien. Ravagers is MCU-only; his Avengers status was honorary during the Korvac Saga and is left out.

name: Chase Stein
caseNote: Subject has no superpowers and fights with the Fistigons, flame-projecting gauntlets taken from his parents' lab. He serves as the Runaways' pilot and mechanic. The equipment was never returned.
notes: Gregg Sulkin played him in Hulu's Runaways, which does not count toward mcu. He briefly used Darkhawk's powers in Avengers Arena; that codename is left out because it belongs mainly to Chris Powell.

name: Colossus
caseNote: Subject converts his body into organic steel, rendering him nearly invulnerable. A Russian farm boy turned X-Men heavy hitter and the usual thrower in the Fastball Special. Agents are advised to stand clear of the throw.
notes: In Deadpool & Wolverine he appears briefly as a CGI character at the start of the film (credited to Stefan Kapičić as voice); counted as on screen, not voice-only. 'Juggernaut' is omitted as an alias because it belongs to Cain Marko.

name: Corvus Glaive
caseNote: Subject is the Black Order's field leader and Thanos's most loyal lieutenant. His namesake glaive grants him immortality. Agents are advised to confiscate the weapon first.

name: Crimson Dynamo
caseNote: Subject designation covers a succession of Soviet and Russian pilots of the same red powered armor, the first built by an expert on electricity. Most have fought Iron Man; some later joined the Winter Guard. Agents should confirm which pilot they are facing.
notes: Legacy mantle with more than a dozen holders: realName gives the original, Anton Vanko, while the Winter Guard link comes from later pilots such as Dmitri Bukharin. mcu is false because no Crimson Dynamo appears on screen; Anton Vanko appears unarmored in Iron Man 2.

name: Crossbones
caseNote: Subject is a mercenary enforcer frequently employed by the Red Skull and Hydra. An expert combatant and marksman who wears a black-and-white skull mask. His stint with the Thunderbolts ended in discharge, which surprised no one.
notes: Debut is the cameo in Captain America #359 listed in Wikipedia's infobox (full appearance #360, named in #362). Energy powers from corrupted Terrigen Mist were temporary, so origin is trained.

name: Cyclops
caseNote: Subject projects concussive optic blasts that only ruby quartz can contain. Founding member and longtime field leader of the X-Men. Agents are advised to stay out of his line of sight.
notes: James Marsden returns in Avengers: Doomsday (Dec 2026) and Kit Connor is cast for the 2028 X-Men film, both after the cutoff, so mcu is false. 'Phoenix' (from Phoenix Five) is omitted as an alias because it belongs to Jean Grey.

name: Dazzler
caseNote: Subject converts sound into light, from stage effects to laser blasts. A singer who launched her career in the disco era and has served with the X-Men and Excalibur. Venue security is advised to bring sunglasses.
notes: excalibur refers to New Excalibur and shield to her later stint as a S.H.I.E.L.D. agent; the infobox's Heralds of Galactus entry is omitted as not a clear main-continuity tenure. Halston Sage's Dark Phoenix cameo is Fox, not MCU.

name: Death
caseNote: Subject is the abstract embodiment of mortality, usually appearing as a hooded skeleton or a dark-haired woman. Has been courted by Thanos and by Deadpool. Agents are reminded that all appointments with Subject are eventually kept.
notes: An abstract entity with no fixed alignment. Set to villain because she usually acts as an antagonist (for example in Agatha All Along), but this is contested. The alias Grim Reaper is left out because it belongs to another game character; Rio Vidal is her MCU disguise.

name: Devil Dinosaur
caseNote: Subject is a red-skinned dinosaur from Dinosaur World, mutated by fire into something stronger and smarter than his kin. He has partnered with Moon-Boy and, later, Moon Girl. Requests to keep him as a pet will be denied.
notes: Origin is mutate because his extra powers came from a fire-triggered mutation; alien (a non-human Devil-Beast from Dinosaur World) is also arguable. His Secret Warriors membership (2017, with Moon Girl) comes from the article body, not the infobox.

name: Doctor Octopus
caseNote: Subject is nuclear physicist Otto Octavius, whose four mechanical arms were fused to his body in a laboratory accident. Founded the Sinister Six. Once spent a period living as Spider-Man in Peter Parker's body and declared himself 'Superior'.
notes: Origin is classed tech because his abilities come from the mechanical arms; the radiation accident fused them to him and gave him mental control (Wikipedia: human mutate/cyborg). Avengers and Hydra memberships come from his time as the Superior Spider-Man and Superior Octopus.

name: Dum Dum Dugan
debutIssue: Sgt. Fury and His Howling Commandos #1
caseNote: Subject is a former circus strongman who served as second-in-command of the Howling Commandos and later as deputy director of S.H.I.E.L.D. Rarely seen without his bowler hat. The hat is not regulation; nobody has raised the issue.
notes: Original Sin (2014) revealed the modern Dugan to be a Life Model Decoy carrying his mind; origin stays trained for his long history as a human soldier.

name: Ebony Maw
caseNote: Subject is the Black Order's chief manipulator, relying on persuasion and mind control rather than brawn. Once compelled Doctor Strange to summon Shuma-Gorath. Agents are advised not to engage Subject in conversation.
notes: The current Wikipedia list entry has no infobox. The cameo debut (New Avengers vol. 3 #8, Sept 2013; full appearance Infinity #1, Oct 2013) comes from the 2023 version of his article.

name: Ego the Living Planet
caseNote: Subject is a sentient planet with a face on its surface and a brain at its core. Has clashed with Thor, Galactus and the Silver Surfer, and once had a starship engine bolted to its south pole. Agents are advised not to land without an invitation.
notes: Debut is a last-page cameo in Thor #132 (full appearance #133). The infobox also lists the Nova Corps, but Ego only briefly joined before taking the Corps over, so it is left out. The Elders of the Universe article counts Ego as an Elder.

name: Electro
caseNote: Subject is Max Dillon, a lineman turned into a living electrical capacitor when lightning struck as he repaired a power line. A founding member of the Sinister Six. Agents should not offer to shake hands.
notes: Francine Frye has also used the Electro name; this entry is Max Dillon. The 'Jolt' alias is left out because it belongs to the Thunderbolts' Jolt.

name: Elixir
caseNote: Subject is a biokinetic mutant who can heal or destroy at the cellular level, and once belonged to the anti-mutant Reavers before his own powers emerged. He later served on Krakoa as one of the Five. A change of perspective is noted.
notes: Here new-mutants means the 2003 New Mutants training squad at the Xavier Institute; he later served in X-Force (2008 series) and as one of Krakoa's resurrection Five.

name: Emma Frost
caseNote: Subject is a powerful telepath who can turn her body into organic diamond. Formerly the White Queen of the Hellfire Club, later a headmistress and co-leader of the X-Men. Agents are reminded that she can hear that.
notes: Antihero follows the rubric's side-switching clause: Wikipedia describes her evolving from supervillain to superhero and quotes a critic calling her Marvel's 'best anti-hero', though hero is arguable. 'Black Queen' and 'Black King' are omitted because they belong primarily to Selene and Sebastian Shaw.

name: Enchantress
caseNote: Subject, Amora, is an Asgardian sorceress specializing in charm and mind control. Joined Baron Zemo's original Masters of Evil alongside the Executioner. Agents should decline any beverage Subject offers.
notes: Enchantress is the alias of both Amora (used here) and Sylvie Lushton. Wikipedia calls the MCU's Sylvie in Loki a different version partially based on the character; Amora has never appeared, so mcu is false but arguable.

name: Eternity
caseNote: Subject is the abstract entity embodying time and the living universe. First contacted by Doctor Strange during his struggle against Baron Mordo and Dormammu. Agents are advised that Subject does not keep office hours.
notes: A neutral cosmic entity, set to hero because it generally helps heroes such as Doctor Strange; contested. First mentioned in Strange Tales #134 (July 1965). Counted as MCU because Wikipedia lists the entity itself, not a statue, in Thor: Love and Thunder.

name: Executioner
caseNote: Subject, Skurge, is an Asgardian half-giant who wields an enchanted double-bladed axe. After years as the Enchantress's enforcer, he died holding the bridge Gjallarbru so his allies could escape Hel. File upgraded posthumously.
notes: A villain for most of his history, but his redemptive death holding Gjallarbru is his most famous story, so antihero is arguable. The Executioner name has also been used by an android and by Daniel DuBois.

name: Falcon (Sam Wilson)
caseNote: Subject flies on a mechanical wing harness and shares a telepathic link with birds, notably his falcon Redwing. Longtime partner of Captain America who later carried the shield himself. Pigeons may be compromised.
notes: 'Captain America' left out of aliases because it belongs primarily to Steve Rogers.

name: Fandral
caseNote: Subject is the swashbuckling swordsman of the Warriors Three, based by Stan Lee on the public persona of Errol Flynn. Charter member of the trio alongside Hogun and Volstagg. A cape is considered standard issue.

name: Firestar
debutIssue: Spider-Man and His Amazing Friends: "The Triumph of the Green Goblin"
caseNote: Subject is a mutant who generates and controls microwave energy and can fly, with service in the New Warriors, the Avengers and the X-Men. She first appeared on Saturday-morning television in 1981. Microwave ovens should not be left unattended.
notes: She debuted on TV (episode aired September 12, 1981); her first canon comics appearance was Uncanny X-Men #193 (May 1985). The nickname 'Angel' is left out of aliases to avoid a clash with Archangel.

name: Forge
caseNote: Subject is a Cheyenne mutant with an intuitive genius for invention, fitted with a bionic hand and leg. Designed the neutralizer that once cost Storm her powers, then joined the X-Men. Agents are advised not to hand him the office printer.
notes: He has no canonical civilian name (Claremont's outline name Daniel Lone Eagle was never used), and the infobox alias 'Maker' is omitted to avoid confusion with the Maker (Ultimate Reed Richards). He relies on gadgets but is classified mutant because his inventive genius is his X-gene power.

name: Frigga
caseNote: Subject is the wife of Odin and Queen of Asgard; she raised Thor and adopted Loki. Has since ruled Asgard as the All-Mother. Her protective spells on her son Balder remain the benchmark for parental supervision.
notes: Later comics rename her Freyja, and the infobox gives her full name as Freyja Freyrdottir. Wikipedia's comics biography calls her Thor's stepmother, though she raised him.

name: Gambit
caseNote: Subject charges objects with kinetic energy, favoring playing cards as the delivery method. A New Orleans thief turned X-Man, later married to Rogue. Agents are advised not to accept a game of cards.
notes: Infobox gives Uncanny X-Men Annual #14 (July 1990) as his published debut and Uncanny X-Men #266 (Aug 1990) as his in-story debut, both 1990. 'Death' (Horseman name) is omitted to avoid the cosmic entity Death.

name: Genis-Vell
caseNote: Subject is the son of the Kree hero Mar-Vell, artificially aged by his mother and given false memories. Has operated as Legacy, Captain Marvel and Photon, and served with the Thunderbolts. Agents are reminded that cosmic awareness is not the same as sanity.
notes: Origin set to alien (Kree and Titanian Eternal hybrid), though his powers largely come from the Nega-Bands and cosmic awareness. The aliases Captain Marvel and Photon are left out because they belong mainly to other game characters.

name: Gertrude Yorkes
caseNote: Subject has no powers of her own but commands Old Lace, a genetically engineered Deinonychus, through a psychic link. Her parents were time-traveling members of the Pride. Pet registration remains outstanding.
notes: Gert has no powers of her own; her ability is a psychic link to Old Lace, a genetically engineered dinosaur, so tech versus trained is debatable. Her infobox gives no cover date (July 2003 matches the other Runaways #1 entries), and Hulu's Runaways does not count toward mcu.

name: Gorr the God Butcher
caseNote: Subject is an alien who lost his family and faith, then took up All-Black the Necrosword and swore revenge on all gods. Hunted deities across past, present and future. Gods are advised to keep a low profile.
notes: Gorr is a mortal alien whose powers come from All-Black the Necrosword, a symbiote, so alien fits on both counts.

name: Green Goblin
caseNote: Subject is industrialist Norman Osborn, whose botched recreation of a strength-enhancing formula gave him superhuman abilities and drove him insane. Attacks from a glider with pumpkin bombs. Was later given command of H.A.M.M.E.R., which replaced S.H.I.E.L.D., with predictable results.
notes: This entry is Norman Osborn; Harry Osborn, Bart Hamilton and Phil Urich have also been the Green Goblin. Primary team is the Dark Avengers he led as Iron Patriot; 'Iron Patriot' is left out of aliases to avoid a clash with War Machine.

name: Gwenpool
caseNote: Subject claims to come from a world where this universe is a comic book, and has worked as a mercenary and with the West Coast Avengers. Her abilities involve awareness of the fourth wall. This memo assumes she is reading it.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox lists her design debut on Chris Bachalo's variant cover (on sale June 2015, cover-dated August 2015) and her first story in Howard the Duck vol. 6 #1 (on sale November 2015, cover-dated January 2016). Origin is trained because she started with no powers beyond knowing the Marvel Universe (fourth-wall abilities came later), and alignment is antihero because of her mercenary start.

name: Hammerhead
caseNote: Subject is a Maggia boss whose shattered skull was rebuilt with metal, leaving the top of his head flat. Dresses in the manner of a 1920s gangster. Agents are advised not to engage him head-on.
notes: Only his first name, Joseph, is known (per The Amazing Spider-Man #618). Origin set to tech for his metal skull and later adamantium implants; before those implants he had no superhuman powers, so 'trained' is arguable.

name: Harry Osborn
caseNote: Subject is the son of Norman Osborn and was Peter Parker's best friend and roommate in college. Has taken up his father's Green Goblin identity on more than one occasion. Chemical storage at Osborn properties is under review.
notes: Alignment is contested: he is mostly Peter's best friend but has been the Green Goblin and Kindred; antihero reflects a character defined by switching sides. His powers came from the Goblin formula, but for long stretches he has none.

name: Havok
caseNote: Subject absorbs ambient cosmic energy and releases it as plasma blasts. Younger brother of Cyclops; has led both X-Factor and the Avengers Unity Squad. Agents are advised not to bring up his brother.
notes: He first appeared as Alex Summers in X-Men #54, and the Havok codename came later in 1969. Lucas Till's portrayals are Fox, not MCU.

name: Hawkeye (Clint Barton)
caseNote: Subject is a former carnival performer and master archer with no superhuman powers. Began as a reluctant criminal before joining the Avengers in 1965. Agents should not challenge him to darts.
notes: Goliath left out of aliases because it belongs primarily to Hank Pym.

name: Hawkeye (Kate Bishop)
caseNote: Subject is a wealthy New Yorker and expert archer with no superhuman powers who shares the Hawkeye title with Clint Barton. Longtime member of the Young Avengers. Agents are advised to specify which Hawkeye they mean.

name: Heimdall
caseNote: Subject is the sole guardian of the Bifrost bridge into Asgard and is described as all-seeing and all-hearing. Brother of Sif. Agents should assume every conversation is being monitored.

name: Hela
caseNote: Subject is the Asgardian goddess of death and rules the realms of Hel and Niflheim. Can kill a mortal or an Asgardian with a single touch. Handshakes are not required by protocol.
notes: Infobox affiliations are the Hell-Lords, Death Gods and Black Order (one storyline); asgard is used for her place in the Asgardian pantheon as ruler of Hel and Niflheim.

name: Hellion
caseNote: Subject is a powerful telekinetic mutant from a wealthy Los Angeles family who trained in the Xavier Institute's Hellions squad. His confidence exceeds recommended limits.
notes: His teams (Hellions, New X-Men) were Xavier Institute student squads with no TEAMS id, and he never served on an X-Men main roster, so primaryTeam is none.

name: Hercules
caseNote: Subject is the Olympian son of Zeus, known as the Prince of Power. Longtime Avenger and a founding member of the Champions of Los Angeles. Reports of his carousing have not been exaggerated.
notes: Debut contested: the infobox lists an in-shadow appearance in U.S.A. Comics #7 (March 1943) first, while the modern character debuted in Journey into Mystery Annual #1 (1965).

name: High Evolutionary
caseNote: Subject is a geneticist who accelerated his own evolution and now operates inside sentient armor. Created the New Men and an entire Counter-Earth. Agents are advised to decline any offer of improvement.
notes: The infobox also gives a mention in Thor #133 (Oct 1966); the first actual appearance, #134, is used here. Origin could be argued as tech because of his armor, but Wikipedia files him as a mutate who experimented on his own genome.

name: Hobgoblin (Roderick Kingsley)
caseNote: Subject is fashion designer Roderick Kingsley, who found one of Norman Osborn's hideouts and perfected a strength formula from his notes. For years a brainwashed Ned Leeds stood in for him as the Hobgoblin. He later licensed the identity to others for a cut.
notes: Roderick_Kingsley redirects to Hobgoblin (Marvel Comics), whose infobox gives only ASM #238 (March 1983); Kingsley appeared in civilian guise earlier in The Spectacular Spider-Man. Others (Ned Leeds, Jason Macendale, Phil Urich) have also been the Hobgoblin.

name: Hogun
caseNote: Subject is the grim, taciturn member of the Warriors Three and a skilled horseman. His look was based on actor Charles Bronson. Subject declined to comment on this report.

name: Honey Badger
caseNote: Subject is an Alchemax clone of Laura Kinney, adopted by Laura as a younger sister. She has a healing factor, one claw per arm and little response to pain. Her enthusiasm remains unclassified.
notes: Wikipedia's entry (in List of Marvel Comics characters: K) gives November 2015, the on-sale month; All-New Wolverine #2 is cover-dated January 2016. Her X-Men membership is Jean Grey's X-Men Red team (2018).

name: Hulk
caseNote: Subject is a physicist caught in the blast of a gamma bomb he helped design. Transforms into a green-skinned powerhouse under emotional stress. Agents are strongly advised not to make him angry.

name: Hulkling
caseNote: Subject is a shapeshifting Kree–Skrull hybrid and a founding member of the Young Avengers. He was later crowned emperor of the Kree–Skrull Alliance. Staff are reminded that he is not the Hulk.
notes: The Kree and Skrull empire ids reflect his reign as Emperor Dorrek VIII of the Kree–Skrull Alliance; a short 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy stint is left out. Marvel chose not to make Billy's boyfriend Eddie in Agatha All Along into Hulkling, so mcu is false.

name: Hydro-Man
caseNote: Subject is a former cargo ship crewman knocked overboard near an experimental undersea generator, after which he could turn his body into water. Has served with the Frightful Four. Agents are advised to keep him away from reservoirs.
notes: His only live-action appearance is the Water Elemental illusion in Spider-Man: Far From Home, which Wikipedia calls a creature inspired by Hydro-Man (the film also name-drops Morris Bench), so the MCU flag is debatable. Infobox Sinister Six and Maggia links lack supporting text and are left out.

name: Hyperion (Marcus Milton)
caseNote: Subject was sent to Earth as an infant, the last survivor of a race of Eternals, and raised by a man he called Father. After his universe was destroyed, he was freed from A.I.M. captivity and joined the Avengers. Comparisons to other caped strongmen are discouraged.
notes: Several Hyperions exist (Zhib-Ran, Mark Milton and others), which invites confusion; this is the Avenger from Hickman's run. He later led the 2015 Squadron Supreme, so the primary team is arguable.

name: Iceman
caseNote: Subject freezes the moisture around him and can convert his body into living ice. Founding member of the X-Men, since described as an Omega-level mutant. Agents are advised to dress warmly.
notes: champions refers to the 1975 Champions of Los Angeles and marauders to Kate Pryde's Krakoa-era crew. Ben Wang is only in talks for the 2028 X-Men film, so mcu is false.

name: Iron Man
caseNote: Subject is a billionaire inventor who built his first armored suit while held captive. Founding member of the Avengers and a former director of S.H.I.E.L.D. Agents are advised that the suit is not available on loan.
notes: Infobox lists the December 1962 on-sale date; the March 1963 cover date given in the article lead is used per rubric.

name: Iron Monger
caseNote: Subject is a ruthless industrialist and champion chess player who bought out Tony Stark's company and renamed it after himself. Later built an oversized suit of armor of his own. Board meetings with Subject are not recommended.
notes: Debut is Obadiah Stane's first appearance; the Iron Monger armor debuted in Iron Man #200 (November 1985).

name: Ironheart
caseNote: Subject is a teenage engineering prodigy who built her own suit of powered armor while a student at MIT. Has fought alongside the Champions. MIT has been notified.
notes: Debut is the cameo in Invincible Iron Man vol. 2 #7 (May 2016), with her full appearance in #9 (July 2016); Wikipedia's lead calls it vol. 3. Avengers and Young Avengers appear only in her infobox and are left out.

name: Jack Flag
caseNote: Subject is an Arizona vigilante who gained superhuman strength after being drenched in Mister Hyde's chemicals. Has aided Captain America and served with the Guardians of the Galaxy. Patriotism is not a registration exemption.

name: Jack O'Lantern
caseNote: Subject is a CIA-trained mercenary who adopted a pumpkin-headed costume, a glider and pumpkin bombs. Later traded the identity for a goblin-themed one. Agents are advised he takes Halloween seriously.
notes: Several characters have used the identity. This record follows the first, Jason Macendale (later the second Hobgoblin; that name is left out of aliases because it belongs to Roderick Kingsley), while later wearers such as Steven Levins have other names and teams.

name: Jackal
caseNote: Subject is Miles Warren, a former Empire State University professor who has cloned Spider-Man more than once. Spliced his own genes with a jackal's to enhance his abilities. Agents are advised to confirm all identities twice.
notes: Debut is Miles Warren's first appearance per the infobox; he first appeared as the Jackal in The Amazing Spider-Man #129 (February 1974). Origin is mutate because his enhanced abilities come from splicing his genes with a jackal's.

name: Jane Foster
caseNote: Subject began as Donald Blake's nurse and later became a doctor. Was deemed worthy of Mjolnir and served as Thor before taking up the mantle of Valkyrie. Thunder may follow any house call.
notes: Origin contested: an ordinary human whose powers came from Mjolnir and later the Valkyrie's All-Weapon (classed magic). 'Thor' and 'Valkyrie' left out of aliases because they belong to other characters in the game.

name: Jean Grey
caseNote: Subject is a telepath and telekinetic of the first rank and the best-known host of the Phoenix Force. Founding member of the X-Men; reported dead on several occasions. Agents should treat any such report as provisional.
notes: Sadie Sink debuted as the MCU's Jean Grey in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (released 2026-07-31). Origin is mutant; the Phoenix Force is an external cosmic entity she has hosted.

name: Jubilee
caseNote: Subject generates explosive energy plasmoids often likened to fireworks. A former mall rat who joined the X-Men in 1989, later enrolled in Generation X and has spent time as a vampire. Agents are advised to keep a safe distance on holidays.

name: Justin Hammer
caseNote: Subject is a British financier who bankrolls costumed criminals in exchange for half of their profits and pays their bail. A persistent business rival of Tony Stark. Subject has no superpowers, merely excellent lawyers.

name: Karnilla
caseNote: Subject is the Norn Queen, a sorceress ruling Nornheim and an ally of Loki. Has long pursued Balder the Brave. Her magic has been rated second only to Odin's among Asgardians.
notes: No standalone article or infobox; debut taken from Wikipedia's List of Marvel Comics characters: K (Journey into Mystery #107). Mostly an enemy of Asgard, but she has occasionally sided with it.

name: Karolina Dean
caseNote: Subject is a Majesdanian alien who absorbs solar energy to fly and project light. She was raised in Los Angeles by actor parents who belonged to the Pride. Agents should bring sunglasses.
notes: Virginia Gardner played her in Hulu's Runaways, which does not count toward mcu.

name: Katie Power
caseNote: Subject is the youngest member of Power Pack, given energy-disintegration powers by a dying Kymellian at age five. She has operated as Energizer and Starstreak. Bedtime remains non-negotiable.
notes: Her powers were handed over by Whitey, a dying Kymellian alien, so alien is the closest fit even though Katie is human (cosmic is arguable). 'Katie Power' redirects to the Power Pack article.

name: Kingpin
caseNote: Subject is a New York crime lord of considerable size, most of it muscle. Has hired the Hand and served as Mayor of New York City. Agents are advised not to comment on his weight.
notes: Team set to the Hand: it is in his infobox, and he controlled the Hand after Shadowland until Superior Spider-Man #14 (2013). The infobox also lists Hydra, Thunderbolts, Sinister Six and Emissaries of Evil with no supporting text, and he briefly held the Hellfire Club's White King seat (Immortal X-Men #14).

name: Kitty Pryde
caseNote: Subject can phase through solid matter, disrupting any electronics she passes through. Joined the X-Men at thirteen and was later accompanied by a small purple dragon named Lockheed. Agents are advised that locked doors are a formality.
notes: hellfire-club reflects her Krakoa-era role as Red Queen of the Hellfire Trading Company. 'Star-Lord' is omitted as an alias because it belongs to Peter Quill.

name: Knull
caseNote: Subject is a primordial god of darkness who created the symbiotes and the living blade All-Black. Once sealed Earth inside a sphere of symbiote dragons. Agents are advised to carry a flashlight.
notes: The infobox lists an unnamed figure in Thor: God of Thunder #6 (March 2013), later identified as Knull, before his full debut in Venom vol. 4 #3 (August 2018), so the debut year is contested. Origin set to deity (a primordial god); Venom: The Last Dance is a Sony film, not MCU.

name: Kraven the Hunter
caseNote: Subject is Sergei Kravinoff, a big-game hunter who regards Spider-Man as the most dangerous game. Maintains superhuman strength and slowed aging with a potion of jungle herbs. Agents should not wear animal print in his presence.
notes: Origin is contested: his potion is described both as a 'mystical serum' and as jungle herbs, and Wikipedia classes him as human mutate. A silhouette of Kraven in the No Way Home sky is not counted as a live-action appearance, and the 2024 film is Sony's.

name: Kurse
caseNote: Subject was the Dark Elf Algrim the Strong until the Beyonder rebuilt him as the armored Kurse. Pursued Thor obsessively over a betrayal that was Malekith's doing. Agents should confirm the target before filing a grudge.
notes: Debuted as Algrim in Thor #347 (Sep 1984) and first appeared as Kurse in Secret Wars II #4 (Oct 1985); the Beyonder's empowerment makes cosmic arguable. He later repented and was granted Asgardian citizenship, and a second Kurse (Waziria) exists.

name: Laufey
caseNote: Subject is king of the Frost Giants and the biological father of Loki. Usually depicted as an enemy of Odin. Family reunions are not recommended.
notes: No standalone article or infobox; debut taken from Wikipedia's List of Marvel Comics characters: L.

name: Living Brain
caseNote: Subject is a robot billed as the most intelligent computer in existence. Has since been reprogrammed as a lab assistant at Parker Industries. Agents are advised to locate the off switch before engaging.
notes: It was briefly part of Boomerang's Marvel NOW! Sinister Six before The Superior Foes of Spider-Man dropped it, so that is treated as a one-off. Wikipedia refers to the robot as 'it'.

name: Living Tribunal
caseNote: Subject is a three-faced cosmic judge charged with keeping balance across the multiverse. Once moved to destroy Earth until Doctor Strange argued the planet's case. Agents are advised not to appeal Subject's rulings.
notes: MCU set to false. Wikipedia calls its Multiverse of Madness moment a cameo, but only statues or heads of the Tribunal are shown there and in Loki. A neutral judge written mostly as 'it', so alignment and gender are contested.

name: Lizard
caseNote: Subject is Dr. Curt Connors, a former army surgeon who lost his right arm and developed a lizard-DNA serum to regrow it. The serum worked, with side effects. Connors and the Lizard do not share priorities.
notes: The infobox lists the Sinister Six, but his comics membership was a one-off during Civil War, so it is not counted.

name: Loki
caseNote: Subject is a Frost Giant by birth, adopted by Odin and raised as Thor's brother. His schemes inadvertently led to the formation of the Avengers. Statements by Subject are not to be entered into the record without corroboration.
notes: Infobox lists a Golden Age Loki in Venus #6 (Aug 1949) ahead of the modern Loki's Journey into Mystery #85 (Oct 1962); the rubric takes the earliest, though most players will expect 1962. Usually a villain with antihero runs, and written as genderfluid at times (Lady Loki, Agent of Asgard, the MCU) though primarily male.

name: Longshot
caseNote: Subject is an artificial lifeform from the Mojoverse whose powers bend probability in his favor, provided his intentions are good. Escaped the television tyrant Mojo and joined the X-Men. Agents are advised not to bet against him.
notes: Wikipedia gives his species as 'Artificial Mojoverse lifeform' and his alter ego as 'No dual identity'. Origin is set to alien (an engineered extradimensional being), though synthetic is arguable and he is not a mutant.

name: Lorelei
caseNote: Subject is an Asgardian and the younger sister of Amora the Enchantress. Has used enchanted golden mead as a love potion. Personnel are advised to bring their own drinks.
notes: Her live-action role in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. does not count toward mcu.

name: M.O.D.O.K.
aliases: Mental Organism Designed Only for Killing
caseNote: Subject underwent A.I.M. mutagenic experiments that vastly enlarged both his intellect and his head. Travels by hoverchair and wields psionic powers. Hat size remains classified.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox gives Tales of Suspense #94 (October 1967), but its lead and publication history name #93 (September 1967) as the first appearance, so #93 is used. The MCU's M.O.D.O.K. is Darren Cross (Corey Stoll), not George Tarleton.

name: Madame Web
caseNote: Subject is Cassandra Webb, a blind clairvoyant and precognitive mutant who long depended on a web-shaped life-support system. Has used her abilities to help Spider-Man on several occasions. Meetings with Subject need not be scheduled; she will already know.
notes: This entry is Cassandra Webb, the original; Julia Carpenter later inherited the name. The 2024 Sony film is not MCU and gives her a spider-bite origin, unlike the comics' mutant.

name: Magik
caseNote: Subject teleports via stepping discs through the demon dimension Limbo, which she rules as its sorceress. Younger sister of Colossus; aged seven years in Limbo while no time passed on Earth. Agents are advised not to follow her through glowing circles.
notes: The 1975 debut is Illyana as a child; the infobox also lists her debut as Magik in Magik #1 (Dec 1983). She is a mutant whose sorcery was acquired in Limbo, and Wikipedia calls her a superhero, though her Darkchilde side could support antihero.

name: Magus
caseNote: Subject is the dark aspect of Adam Warlock and has ruled the Universal Church of Truth. Has repeatedly tried to claim the Infinity Gems. Agents are advised that Subject is, quite literally, his own worst enemy.
notes: The name is ambiguous: Wikipedia's 'Magus (Marvel Comics)' is the Technarch father of Warlock (New Mutants #18, 1984). Given this cosmic batch, this record is Adam Warlock's evil self, covered in the Adam Warlock article without an infobox; the debut is from its Strange Tales #178 citation.

name: Malekith
caseNote: Subject rules the Dark Elves of Svartalfheim and has often wielded the Casket of Ancient Winters. Served as the main antagonist of the War of the Realms. Agents should not accept faerie food from Subject.
notes: Dark Elves are treated as a Norse mythological race (deity).

name: Man-Wolf
caseNote: Subject is astronaut John Jameson, son of J. Jonah Jameson. A gem he found on the Moon turns him into a wolf-like creature. Agents are advised not to schedule meetings during a full moon.
notes: The infobox debut is John Jameson's first appearance; he first became Man-Wolf in ASM #124 (September 1973). Alignment and origin are judgment calls: Jameson is a supporting hero (astronaut, Stargod, Agents of Wakanda), while his Man-Wolf form is a monster powered by the mystical Godstone.

name: Mandarin
caseNote: Subject is a master martial artist whose ten rings, salvaged from a crashed alien starship, each grant a different power. A longtime nemesis of Iron Man. Agents are advised to count the rings before engaging.
notes: mcuFirst is contested: Iron Man 3 has the Mandarin persona (Trevor Slattery as figurehead, Aldrich Killian claiming the title), while Shang-Chi's Xu Wenwu is the closer adaptation but never uses the name himself. The comics never reveal his birth name, so realName is empty.

name: Mangog
caseNote: Subject embodies the hatred of a billion billion beings whose race was defeated by Odin. Has repeatedly sought the Odinsword to end the universe. Subject claims he will exist as long as there is hatred; the bureau has no rebuttal.
notes: Origin is a judgment call: a spell-made living prison embodying an alien race's hatred; magic chosen, alien arguable.

name: Maria Hill
caseNote: Subject is a career intelligence officer who succeeded Nick Fury as director of S.H.I.E.L.D. Has no superhuman abilities and has repeatedly clashed with the Avengers over oversight. Agents should expect an audit.
notes: Infobox lists March 2005 (on-sale date); the April 2005 cover date is used per rubric.

name: Martinex
caseNote: Subject is the last surviving Pluvian, with crystalline skin engineered for Pluto's harsh conditions. Founding member of the original Guardians of the Galaxy and its resident scientist. Do not mistake Subject for a chandelier.
notes: Pluvians are genetically engineered descendants of human colonists, classed as alien. Ravagers is MCU-only; his Avengers status was honorary during the Korvac Saga and is left out.

name: Marvel Boy (Noh-Varr)
caseNote: Subject is a Kree soldier from an alternate universe, enhanced with insect DNA, who once declared war on Earth. He has since served with the Avengers and the Young Avengers. The declaration remains on file.
notes: He began as a hostile alien who declared war on Earth and served briefly on Osborn's Dark Avengers before turning heroic; inhumans reflects his time with the Royals. Primary team is the Young Avengers (as Marvel Boy), though as Protector he was also a main-roster Avenger; 'Captain Marvel' is left out of aliases.

name: Mercury
caseNote: Subject is a mutant whose body is a liquid metal resembling mercury, which she can reshape or solidify at will. She trained in the Xavier Institute's Hellions squad. Thermometer jokes are discouraged.
notes: Her teams (Hellions, New X-Men) were Xavier Institute student squads with no TEAMS id, and she never served on an X-Men main roster, so primaryTeam is none.

name: Mister Hyde
caseNote: Subject is Calvin Zabo, a medical researcher who drew on Jekyll and Hyde to create a formula that turns him into a hulking brute. Has served on several Masters of Evil rosters and the Thunderbolts. Agents are advised his bedside manner has not improved.
notes: Calvin Johnson in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. does not count for the MCU field because it is an ABC/Marvel Television series.

name: Mister Negative
debutIssue: Free Comic Book Day: The Amazing Spider-Man #1
caseNote: Subject runs a Chinatown soup kitchen as philanthropist Martin Li while leading the Inner Demons gang as Mister Negative. An experimental drug gave him control of the Darkforce and Lightforce. Agents are advised to check both sides of his ledger.
notes: Martin Li is the civilian identity he lives under; Wikipedia says his birth name was never revealed. Spider-Man: Brand New Day only references his gang's logo, so he does not count as appearing.

name: Mockingbird
caseNote: Subject is a biologist and former S.H.I.E.L.D. Agent 19 who fights with battle staves. Founding member of the West Coast Avengers and ex-wife of Hawkeye. Was once declared dead; records were later amended.
notes: Origin contested: a non-powered agent for most of her history, she later gained superhuman abilities from a Super-Soldier Serum/Infinity Formula mix (classed super-soldier). The MCU's 'Agent 19' is Laura Barton, and ABC's Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. does not count.

name: Moira MacTaggert
caseNote: Subject is a Scottish geneticist who ran the Muir Island research facility and spent decades treating mutants. Her file was later amended to classify her as a mutant herself. Agents should not assume this file is final.
notes: She was a non-powered human scientist for most of her history until House of X (2019) revealed her as a reincarnating mutant, and she later turned against mutants with Orchis before being depowered. Origin (mutant vs trained) and alignment (hero vs villain) are both contested.

name: Molly Hayes
caseNote: Subject is the youngest founding member of the Runaways, a mutant with superhuman strength and invulnerability. She is known for her hats. Agents should not mistake her age for weakness.
notes: Allegra Acosta played her in Hulu's Runaways, which does not count toward mcu.

name: Molten Man
caseNote: Subject was coated in an experimental liquid metal alloy during a lab accident, leaving him with metallic skin and heat powers. Is the stepbrother of Liz Allan. Agents are advised not to shake hands.
notes: His only live-action appearance is the Fire Elemental illusion in Spider-Man: Far From Home, which Wikipedia describes as a creature based on Molten Man rather than Mark Raxton himself, so the MCU flag is debatable.

name: Monica Rambeau
caseNote: Subject is a former New Orleans harbor patrol lieutenant who can transform into any form of energy. Led the Avengers in the 1980s as Captain Marvel. Agents should confirm her current codename before filing.
notes: Sources disagree on the annual's month (Wikipedia infobox: October 1982; dealer listings: December 1982), so a year-only date is used. 'Captain Marvel' left out of aliases because the game assigns it to Carol Danvers.

name: Montana
caseNote: Subject is Jackson Brice, a marksman and lariat specialist with the Enforcers. Has spent decades as hired muscle for New York crime bosses. Agents are advised that the cowboy hat is not a disguise.
notes: His MCU appearance is Jackson Brice (Logan Marshall-Green) as the first Shocker in Spider-Man: Homecoming. 'Shocker' is left out of aliases because it belongs to Herman Schultz.

name: Moon Girl
caseNote: Subject is a preteen Inhuman inventor who can swap minds with her partner, Devil Dinosaur. Amadeus Cho has called her the smartest person in the world. Classroom visits should allow for a dinosaur.
notes: Wikipedia has no character infobox: her page redirects to the series article, which gives the November 2015 on-sale launch, while issue #1 is cover-dated January 2016. The animated series makes her human, but in the comics she is an Inhuman.

name: Morbius
caseNote: Subject is Michael Morbius, a Nobel Prize-winning biochemist who tried to cure a rare blood disease with vampire bat DNA and electroshock. He survived as a pseudo-vampire who must drink human blood. Blood drives in his vicinity should be postponed.
notes: Primary team could also be the Legion of Monsters (founding member, 2011 series); the Midnight Sons was chosen for his core role in the 1992 crossover. The 2022 Morbius film is Sony's, not MCU.

name: Morg
caseNote: Subject is a former court executioner who betrayed his own people before Galactus made him a herald. Wields the Power Cosmic and a double-bladed axe. Agents are advised not to request a reference.

name: Morlun
caseNote: Subject is a psychic vampire of extreme age who feeds on the life force of spider-totems. Has hunted Spider-Man and his counterparts across the multiverse with his family, the Inheritors. Agents with spider-powers should request desk duty.

name: Ms. Marvel (Kamala Khan)
caseNote: Subject is a Jersey City teenager and devoted Avengers fan whose powers emerged when the Terrigen Mists spread. Can stretch, shrink and embiggen at will. Co-founded the Champions; her fan fiction remains under review.
notes: Origin contested: Inhuman via Terrigenesis in comics (classed inhuman), but a 2023 retcon added a dormant X-gene and the MCU portrays her as a mutant. Debut uses the background cameo the infobox lists (full debut: All-New Marvel Now! Point One #1, 2014).

name: Mysterio
caseNote: Subject is Quentin Beck, a special-effects artist and stuntman who turned his illusions to crime after his film career stalled. Has no superhuman powers, only smoke, holograms and a fishbowl helmet. Nothing Subject shows you should be believed.
notes: Others have used the Mysterio identity; this entry is Quentin Beck.

name: Nick Fury
debutIssue: Sgt. Fury and His Howling Commandos #1
caseNote: Subject is a World War II veteran who led the Howling Commandos before directing S.H.I.E.L.D. for decades. The Infinity Formula has slowed his aging considerably. Agents are advised not to ask about the eyepatch.
notes: Classed super-soldier under the rubric's Infinity Formula rule, but the MCU version has no enhancements, so origin is contested. Record follows the original Nicholas Joseph Fury, not Nick Fury Jr.

name: Nico Minoru
caseNote: Subject is a sorceress who draws the Staff of One from her body when she bleeds, and is generally accepted as leader of the Runaways. Her parents were dark wizards in the Pride. The family business was declined.
notes: Lyrica Okano played her in Hulu's Runaways, a Marvel Television series that does not count toward mcu.

name: Night Thrasher
caseNote: Subject is an unpowered armored vigilante who founded the New Warriors and financed them through his family's foundation. He rides a skateboard into combat. Agents are advised it is not a toy.
notes: This entry is Dwayne Taylor; his brother Donyell later took the name. He uses armor and gadgets but has no powers, so origin is trained.

name: Nightcrawler
caseNote: Subject teleports short distances, leaving behind a puff of brimstone-scented smoke. A devout Catholic, former circus acrobat and veteran of the X-Men and Excalibur. Agents are advised to ventilate the room.
notes: Alan Cumming's MCU appearance is in Avengers: Doomsday (Dec 2026), after the cutoff, so mcu is false.

name: Nikki Gold
caseNote: Subject is a 31st-century Mercurian rescued by the Guardians of the Galaxy from an abandoned spacecraft. Flames radiating from her scalp double as a weapon. Agents are advised to keep extinguishers within reach.
notes: Mercurians are genetically engineered descendants of human colonists, classed as alien. Her Avengers status was honorary during the Korvac Saga and is left out.

name: Northstar
caseNote: Subject flies at superhuman speed and generates light when holding hands with his twin sister, Aurora. Founding member of Alpha Flight and one of the first openly gay superheroes in American comics. Agents should note he is also a world-class skier.
notes: The infobox's Hydra affiliation is omitted because he served only while brainwashed.

name: Odin
caseNote: Subject is the All-Father, ruler of Asgard and father of Thor. Sacrificed his right eye to Mimir in exchange for wisdom. Subject is unavailable for 24 hours each year during the Odinsleep.
notes: First mentioned in Journey into Mystery #85 (Oct 1962); the infobox gives #86 as his first appearance. His place in the prehistoric Avengers of 1,000,000 BC is kept out of the avengers id.

name: Overdrive
debutIssue: Free Comic Book Day: The Amazing Spider-Man #1
caseNote: Subject is a getaway driver who can turn any vehicle into a high-powered one. Has worked for Mister Negative and served in Boomerang's Sinister Six. Agents are advised to note his license plate.
notes: His infobox says 'Free Comic Book Day: Spider-Man (July 2007)', but the article's publication history and Mister Negative's article date this same 'Swing Shift' issue to May 2007. Origin set to tech because his vehicle-modifying power works through nanites.

name: Patriot (Eli Bradley)
mcuFirst: The Falcon and the Winter Soldier
caseNote: Subject is the grandson of Isaiah Bradley and a founding member of the Young Avengers. His first powers came from an illegal street drug; his later ones from a transfusion of his grandfather's blood. The first method is not endorsed.
notes: Eli first faked powers with Mutant Growth Hormone; a transfusion from Isaiah Bradley later gave him real Super-Soldier abilities. In the MCU he appears as civilian Eli Bradley (Elijah Richardson), not as Patriot.

name: Peggy Carter
caseNote: Subject fought with the French Resistance during World War II and later served S.H.I.E.L.D. for many years. Was Captain America's wartime sweetheart. Agents are reminded she was doing this job before most of them were born.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox lists her first, unnamed and obscured, in Tales of Suspense #75 (March 1966); she was first named in 1973. The infobox's Avengers link was a support-staff role and is omitted; the Strategic Scientific Reserve is her MCU agency.

name: Pepper Potts
caseNote: Subject began as Tony Stark's secretary and has since helped run his company. Has taken the field in powered armor of her own. Subject's patience with Mr. Stark is considered her greatest power.
notes: Origin is tech for the Rescue armor and the chest-mounted device that leads Wikipedia to class her as a cyborg. The Avengers entry in her infobox is not supported by the comics text, so it is left out.

name: Phil Coulson
caseNote: Subject is a S.H.I.E.L.D. agent first encountered on the Iron Man case. Noted for composure under fire and a prized set of vintage Captain America trading cards. Reports of Subject's death have repeatedly proven unreliable.
notes: Created for the 2008 Iron Man film; his comics debut is Battle Scars #6 (April 2012). Classed as a hero overall, though the comics version later served Mephisto, led the Squadron Supreme of America and was the main villain of Heroes Reborn (2021).

name: Pip the Troll
caseNote: Subject is a Laxidazian prince turned troll by mutagenic ale. Has served with the Infinity Watch and X-Factor Investigations, and once kept the Space Gem between his toes. Agents are advised to inspect all footwear.
notes: The infobox dates Strange Tales #179 to February 1975, but the Adam Warlock article cites it as April 1975 (#178 was February). Best known for the Infinity Watch; X-Factor Investigations is his only membership on the TEAMS list. He appears in Eternals as a CGI character voiced by Patton Oswalt.

name: Polaris
caseNote: Subject controls magnetism and is known for her green hair. Daughter of Magneto and a longtime member of X-Factor. Agents are advised to remove all metal before the interview.
notes: Primary team is X-Factor (government X-Factor, leader of All-New X-Factor, Krakoa-era X-Factor), though she has also served on X-Men rosters. Emma Dumont's role in The Gifted is Fox TV, not MCU.

name: Prodigy (David Alleyne)
caseNote: Subject is a mutant who absorbed the knowledge and skills of those around him, and kept what he had learned after losing his powers on M-Day. He later served with the Young Avengers and X-Factor. This office envies his study habits.
notes: Here new-mutants means Danielle Moonstar's 2003 New Mutants training squad at the Xavier Institute. He lost his powers on M-Day and got them back through Krakoa's resurrection protocols.

name: Professor X
mcuFirst: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
caseNote: Subject is among the world's most powerful telepaths and founded the X-Men at his school in Westchester, New York. Has relied on a wheelchair for much of his career. Agents are advised that he already knows why they called.
notes: Patrick Stewart played Earth-838's Charles Xavier in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness; his Avengers: Doomsday return (Dec 2026) is after the cutoff. 'Onslaught' is omitted as an alias because Onslaught is a separate game character.

name: Prowler (Hobie Brown)
caseNote: Subject is an inventor who built the Prowler gear after being fired from his window-washing job and first used it as a thief. Spider-Man unmasked him and advised him to rethink his life; he has been an ally since. Agents should not underestimate window washers.
notes: Not the MCU Prowler (Aaron Davis) or Spider-Punk, the Earth-138 Hobie Brown; this Hobie Brown has never appeared in live action, so players are likely to confuse the entries.

name: Proxima Midnight
caseNote: Subject is a Black Order enforcer armed with a spear forged from a star that homes in on its target. Married to fellow Order member Corvus Glaive. Agents should not assume they can outrun the spear.
notes: Wikipedia now covers her in a list entry with no infobox. The debut comes from the entry text (New Avengers #8, September 2013), which matches the infobox of the 2023 version of her article.

name: Psylocke (Betsy Braddock)
caseNote: Subject is a British telepath able to focus her power into a psychic knife. Twin sister of Captain Britain, a title she later took on herself, and a longtime member of the X-Men and X-Force. Agents are advised not to think too loudly.
notes: Her MCU credit is an uncredited alternate-timeline Psylocke (Ayesha Hussain) in Deadpool & Wolverine, listed in Wikipedia's Betsy Braddock in other media article. 'Captain Britain' is omitted as an alias because it belongs primarily to Brian Braddock.

name: Puma
caseNote: Subject is Thomas Fireheart, a mercenary and CEO bred by his tribe to be a perfect warrior. Transforms into an anthropomorphic mountain lion. Once bought the Daily Bugle to repay a debt of honor.
notes: Alignment is contested: he began as an assassin hired to kill Spider-Man, later became an ally and Outlaws member, and has slipped back into mercenary villainy. His powers come from genetic engineering combined with tribal mysticism; origin set to magic.

name: Quicksilver
caseNote: Subject moves at superhuman speed and is the twin brother of the Scarlet Witch. Former Brotherhood of Mutants member who later served with the Avengers and X-Factor. Patience is not among his documented abilities.
notes: Origin contested: portrayed as Magneto's mutant son for decades, but a 2015 retcon (and the MCU) attribute his powers to experiments; classed mutate.

name: Rachel Summers
caseNote: Subject is a telepath and telekinetic from a dystopian future, the daughter of Cyclops and Jean Grey. Has hosted the Phoenix Force and served with the X-Men and Excalibur. Agents are advised not to ask how the future turns out.
notes: 'Phoenix' and 'Marvel Girl', which she has also used, are omitted as aliases because they belong primarily to Jean Grey.

name: Red Guardian
caseNote: Subject is a former Soviet test pilot and KGB agent trained as his nation's answer to Captain America. Was once married to the Black Widow. His throwing disc doubles as a belt buckle.
notes: Record follows Alexei Shostakov, the MCU's Red Guardian, in a mantle with several holders. Comics Alexei has no superhuman powers, but MCU tie-in material presents him as a Soviet super-soldier, so origin is contested.

name: Red Hulk
caseNote: Subject is a career general who spent years hunting the Hulk before becoming a red gamma giant himself. Radiates heat, absorbs energy, and has led the Thunderbolts. The irony has been noted for the record.
notes: Record treats Red Hulk as Thaddeus Ross, so debut and mcuFirst follow Ross (Wikipedia's Red Hulk mantle article has no infobox). As Red Hulk he debuted in Hulk vol. 2 #1 (2008) and first appeared on screen in Captain America: Brave New World (2025).

name: Red She-Hulk
caseNote: Subject is a general's daughter and Bruce Banner's wife who was transformed by gamma radiation into a red-skinned powerhouse. Has served with the Defenders. Family gatherings are considered high-risk.
notes: Wikipedia's Red She-Hulk redirects to Betty Ross, so debut and MCU follow Betty (the infobox says March 1962, but The Incredible Hulk #1 is cover-dated May 1962). She first became Red She-Hulk in Hulk vol. 2 #15 (September 2009) and has never appeared in that form in live action.

name: Red Skull
caseNote: Subject is a Nazi operative with a face like a crimson skull and the archenemy of Captain America. Has commanded Hydra and favors a poison known as the dust of death. Agents are advised to decline all handshakes.
notes: Origin is contested: the comics Johann Shmidt is unpowered for most of his history, but super-soldier fits the MCU's early Super-Soldier Serum and his comics years in a Super-Soldier-derived clone body. Wikipedia dates the Red Skull to Captain America Comics #1 (1941), where George Maxon wore the identity.

name: Rhino
caseNote: Subject is Aleksei Sytsevich, a low-ranking Russian mobster who volunteered for chemical and radiation treatments. They left him with superhuman strength and a rhinoceros-shaped polymer suit. Agents are advised to step aside.
notes: Thunderbolts membership comes from Wilson Fisk's teams in King in Black and Devil's Reign. His live-action films (The Amazing Spider-Man 2, Kraven the Hunter) are Sony productions, not MCU.

name: Rocket Racer
caseNote: Subject is Robert Farrell, a Brooklyn native and eldest of seven children who rides a self-built rocket skateboard. Began as a thief but reformed after run-ins with Spider-Man. Agents are advised he does not stay off the sidewalk.
notes: He debuted as a thief but reformed after early clashes with Spider-Man and later trained with the Initiative and Avengers Academy, so he is set to hero. He has no standalone Wikipedia article.

name: Rockslide
caseNote: Subject is a mutant who forms a rock body from surrounding earth and can reassemble after being shattered. He trained at the Xavier Institute and served with the Young X-Men. Demolition requests should be routed through proper channels.
notes: His teams were Xavier Institute student squads with no TEAMS id, and he never served on an X-Men main roster, so primaryTeam is none.

name: Rogue
caseNote: Subject absorbs the memories and abilities of anyone she touches. Formerly of the Brotherhood of Evil Mutants, later a mainstay of the X-Men and the Avengers Unity Squad. Handshakes are not recommended.
notes: She began as a Brotherhood villain before joining the X-Men, but is classified hero overall. Her surname is unrevealed in canon, and Inde Navarrette's casting is for the 2028 X-Men film.

name: Sandman
caseNote: Subject is career criminal William Baker, alias Flint Marko, whose body turned to sand after exposure to irradiated sand at a nuclear test site. A founding member of both the Sinister Six and the Frightful Four. Agents should check their shoes after any encounter.
notes: Wikipedia notes he later became an antihero (Avengers reserve, Wild Pack, Outlaws), but he has spent most of his history as a villain; the brief Avengers reserve stint is not counted. His birth name is William Baker; Flint Marko is an alias.

name: Scarlet Spider (Ben Reilly)
caseNote: Subject is a clone of Peter Parker grown by the Jackal, who named himself after Uncle Ben and Aunt May's maiden name. Took over as Spider-Man in the mid-1990s while both men believed Parker was the clone. The matter has since been settled; agents should not reopen it.
notes: Debut uses the 1975 clone listed first in the infobox; he returned as Ben Reilly/Scarlet Spider in 1994. Wikipedia calls him a superhero, but he has had villainous turns as the Jackal and Chasm, and his New Warriors stint was brief.

name: Scarlet Witch
caseNote: Subject wields chaos magic capable of altering reality. Former Brotherhood of Mutants member who joined the Avengers in 1965 and later married the Vision. Probability is not to be relied upon in her presence.
notes: Origin contested: introduced as a mutant, retconned in 2015 as a High Evolutionary experiment subject, and now written (as in the MCU) as a chaos-magic witch; classed magic. MCU debut is the Winter Soldier mid-credits scene.

name: Scorpion
caseNote: Subject is Mac Gargan, a private investigator hired by J. Jonah Jameson, who then funded an untested procedure to make him a match for Spider-Man. It granted scorpion-like abilities and a mechanical tail but damaged his mind. Mr. Jameson's research funding is under review.
notes: Debut uses Mac Gargan's first appearance (ASM #19, December 1964); he became the Scorpion in ASM #20 (January 1965). His Dark Avengers and Thunderbolts tenures were as Venom, and he first appears as the Scorpion on screen in Brand New Day (2026).

name: Scream
caseNote: Subject is Donna Diego, a Life Foundation volunteer bonded to one of five symbiotes forcibly spawned from Venom. Uses her prehensile hair as a weapon. Agents are advised that the codename is descriptive.
notes: The Scream symbiote has had several hosts; this record follows the original, Donna Diego.

name: Sentry
caseNote: Subject derives the power of a million exploding suns from an experimental serum. Has served with the New Avengers and the Dark Avengers. A dark counterpart called the Void is attached to his file and should not be engaged.
notes: Infobox gives only the year; the article's citations date the original miniseries September 2000 to January 2001. 'World Breaker' left out of aliases because it belongs primarily to Hulk.

name: Sharon Carter
caseNote: Subject is a veteran S.H.I.E.L.D. field agent known by a numbered code name. A longtime partner of Captain America and kin to a celebrated World War II heroine. Family reunions are classified.
notes: Avengers membership is via the 2010 Secret Avengers and Thunderbolts via Bucky Barnes's 2023 team. The MCU version is revealed as the Power Broker in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, but she is a hero across her history.

name: She-Hulk
caseNote: Subject is an attorney who gained gamma-powered strength from an emergency blood transfusion from her cousin, Bruce Banner. Has served with the Avengers and the Fantastic Four. Known to address the reader directly; agents should not be alarmed.
notes: Infobox lists November 1979 (on-sale date); the February 1980 cover date is used per rubric.

name: Shocker
caseNote: Subject is Herman Schultz, a self-taught engineer who built vibro-shock gauntlets after being jailed and used them to escape. Wears a foam-lined suit to absorb the vibrations. Agents should stand well back.
notes: Two men were the Shocker in Homecoming (Jackson Brice, then Herman Schultz played by Bokeem Woodbine); this entry is Schultz.

name: Shriek
caseNote: Subject is a mutant whose powers were awakened by exposure to Cloak's Darkforce. Projects sonic blasts and draws out the darkness in others. Agents are advised she has no indoor voice.

name: Sif
