caseNote: Subject is a leading Asgardian warrior and Thor's companion since childhood. Born with golden hair, which turned black after Loki cut it and replaced it with dwarf-made hair. Loki is barred from the salon.

name: Silk
caseNote: Subject was bitten by the same radioactive spider as Peter Parker, then spent years locked in a facility for her own protection. Shoots webbing from her fingertips and has a danger sense stronger than Parker's. Agents should not offer to lock any doors for her.
notes: MCU status rests on Cindy Moon appearing as Peter's classmate (Tiffany Espensen) from Homecoming on, never as Silk. Wikipedia lists April 2014 (on-sale month) for the cameo; the issue's cover date is June 2014, and her full appearance is #4.

name: Silver Sable
caseNote: Subject is a Symkarian mercenary who leads the Wild Pack and runs Silver Sable International, which hunts war criminals for a fee. Has no superhuman powers and has been both ally and opponent to Spider-Man. Agents should request a quote in advance.
notes: Wikipedia gives her real name as Silvija Sablinova (older sources: Silver Sablinova). The infobox lists Heroes for Hire, but the article only shows her fighting them, so it is omitted.

name: Silvermane
caseNote: Subject is a Maggia don nicknamed for his near-white hair. Has pursued immortality through a youth formula and, later, a cyborg body. Agents are advised that retirement is not in his plans.
notes: Origin set to tech for his cyborg bodies; he began as an unpowered elderly mob boss relying on a youth formula. Hydra comes from his infobox (alias 'Supreme Hydra') and Hydra's former-member list, though the text only says he sought to lead Hydra. 'Supreme Hydra' is left out of aliases because it belongs mainly to Baron Strucker.

name: Speed
debutIssue: The Vision and the Scarlet Witch vol. 2 #12
caseNote: Subject is a mutant speedster and the twin brother of Wiccan. The Young Avengers found him held in a juvenile facility after he reportedly vaporized his school. Interviews should be brief; Subject will not wait.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox lists the infant Thomas Maximoff's first appearance (Vision and the Scarlet Witch #12, Sept 1986), while Tommy Shepherd debuted in Young Avengers #10 (Mar 2006). The infobox also lists the Champions, but the article describes no such membership.

name: Speedball
caseNote: Subject was struck by extradimensional energy at a research lab, leaving him wrapped in bouncing kinetic force fields. A founding New Warrior, he later operated as Penance. The spiked suit is no longer required.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox says 'January 1988', but the annual has no cover month and other references date it to later in 1988, so debutDate gives the year only. His Thunderbolts membership was as Penance.

name: Spider-Girl (Anya Corazon)
caseNote: Subject was mortally wounded in a clash between two mystical clans and saved by a Spider Society ritual that granted her spider-powers. Operated as Araña before taking the Spider-Girl name. The Spider Society is not a book club.
notes: Origin is contested: her first powers came from a Spider Society mystical ritual, while her later spider-powers came from the Jackal's Spider-Island virus; Wikipedia classes her as human mutate. Her only live-action role is in Sony's Madame Web (2024), not MCU.

name: Spider-Girl (Mayday Parker)
caseNote: Subject is the teenage daughter of Peter Parker and Mary Jane Watson in the alternate MC2 reality. Inherited her father's spider-powers and became Spider-Girl, at first hindered and then helped by her worried parents. Curfew violations are presumed.
notes: Her powers are inherited from Peter Parker rather than gained in an accident; mutate follows Wikipedia's 'human mutate'. Her reserve status with MC2's A-Next is not counted as Avengers membership.

name: Spider-Gwen
caseNote: Subject is the Gwen Stacy of Earth-65, where she, not Peter Parker, was bitten by the radioactive spider. Has operated as Spider-Woman and Ghost-Spider and drums for a band called the Mary Janes. Agents should confirm which Gwen Stacy they are addressing.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox gives September 2014, the on-sale month; CGC lists the November 2014 cover date. Her Spider-Woman codename is left out of aliases because it belongs to Jessica Drew.

name: Spider-Ham
debutIssue: Marvel Tails Starring Peter Porker, the Spectacular Spider-Ham #1
caseNote: Subject was born a spider and was bitten by scientist May Porker after she irradiated herself with an atomic-powered hairdryer, turning him into an anthropomorphic pig with spider-powers. Agents are reminded that he is, in fact, a pig.

name: Spider-Man (Miles Morales)
caseNote: Subject was bitten by a genetically engineered spider and took up the Spider-Man name after the apparent death of his universe's Peter Parker. Can turn invisible and deliver a paralyzing 'venom strike'. Agents should not assume there is only one Spider-Man.
notes: Primary team is the Champions (founding member, longest tenure) rather than the All-New, All-Different Avengers; in the MCU he is only alluded to, never shown. Wikipedia's August 2011 is the on-sale month (released 3 August 2011); dealer listings suggest an October 2011 cover date that I could not confirm from a source I could open.

name: Spider-Man (Peter Parker)
caseNote: Subject gained spider-like abilities after a radioactive spider bit him at a science exhibit. Has sold photographs of himself to the Daily Bugle, which routinely labels him a menace. Agents are advised not to ask who took the pictures.
notes: Teams follow the Wikipedia infobox: fantastic-four reflects his 2011 Future Foundation/FF membership and web-warriors the Spider-Army of the Spider-Verse events.

name: Spider-Man 2099
caseNote: Subject is Miguel O'Hara, a geneticist of the year 2099 whose DNA was half-rewritten with spider genes in an accident at Alchemax. Has talons, venomous fangs and the ability to see in darkness. Reports he files are dated 2099; this is not a clerical error.
notes: Debut is the preview in ASM #365; his first full appearance is Spider-Man 2099 #1 (November 1992). The infobox lists only Exiles and Alchemax; web-warriors reflects his Spider-Army role in the 2014 Spider-Verse event.

name: Spider-Slayer (Alistair Smythe)
caseNote: Subject is the son of Spencer Smythe and continues the family business of building robots to destroy Spider-Man. Wears a bio-organic carapace that restored his ability to walk. Agents are advised the business has one target.
notes: His only live-action role is in Sony's The Amazing Spider-Man 2, which does not count for the MCU.

name: Spider-Woman (Jessica Drew)
caseNote: Subject gained spider-like powers through her scientist father's experiments. Recruited by Hydra before defecting, she later served S.H.I.E.L.D. and S.W.O.R.D. Her pheromones may impair agents' judgment.
notes: A 2006 retcon changed her spider-blood serum origin to a spider-DNA laser experiment; both are mutate. No live-action MCU appearance (her only film role is the animated, Sony-made Across the Spider-Verse).

name: Spot
caseNote: Subject is a scientist who, while working for the Kingpin, tried to replicate Cloak's teleportation and ended up covered in portals. Can reach through his spots to strike from anywhere. Agents are advised not to treat him as a villain of the week.
notes: Debut uses the infobox's listing of his appearance as an unnamed man in #97; he first appeared as the Spot in #98 (January 1985). Wikipedia spells his first name inconsistently (Jonathon/Johnathon), so the common spelling Jonathan is used and the variants are aliases.

name: Squirrel Girl
caseNote: Subject has the combined powers of squirrel and girl, including a prehensile tail and fluency in squirrel. In her first recorded engagement she helped Iron Man defeat Doctor Doom. Agents should not underestimate the squirrels.
notes: Wikipedia calls her a human mutate: her squirrel traits have no stated cause, and later stories say she is not a mutant, so origin is debatable. The cover date is 'Winter 1991', so no month is given; primary team is the Great Lakes Avengers, though she later served on the New Avengers and U.S.Avengers.

name: Starhawk
caseNote: Subject is a 31st-century hero fated to relive his own life repeatedly, and calls himself the One Who Knows. Shares a long, strained history with his adoptive sister Aleta. Agents should assume Subject has read this memo before.
notes: Wikipedia's lead calls him an antihero, but he is filed as a superhero. His powers come from the Arcturan Hawk God, so origin is set to cosmic. Ravagers is an MCU-only affiliation; the 1969 Guardians were only honorary Avengers (Korvac Saga), so that is left out.

name: Stature
caseNote: Subject is the daughter of Scott Lang and a size-changing member of the Young Avengers. Her abilities stem from years of secretly taking her father's Pym Particles. Agents are reminded to secure their Pym Particles.
notes: The debut is Cassie Lang's first appearance as a child; she first became Stature in Young Avengers #6. In the comics her powers come from Pym Particle exposure (mutate), while the MCU version uses a suit.

name: Stegron
caseNote: Subject is a former S.H.I.E.L.D. agent who studied Savage Land dinosaur DNA with Curt Connors, then injected himself with it. Now transforms into a bipedal stegosaurus that can command dinosaurs. Agents are advised to secure all museum fossils.

name: Storm
caseNote: Subject commands weather on a planetary scale and has led the X-Men in the field. Has also served with the Avengers and the Fantastic Four, and reigned as Queen of Wakanda. Agents are advised not to schedule picnics.
notes: No live-action MCU appearance by the cutoff; Maya Boyd is cast for the 2028 X-Men film. wakanda reflects her tenure as Queen of Wakanda.

name: Sunfire
caseNote: Subject ionizes matter into superheated plasma, which also lets him fly. A Japanese mutant who quit the X-Men after a single mission in 1975 and later served with the Avengers Unity Squad. Agents are advised not to ask him for a light.
notes: He began as a nationalist antagonist and quit the X-Men after one mission, but was later elected to the Krakoa-era X-Men and served in Uncanny Avengers. Hero and x-men as primary team are judgment calls.

name: Supergiant
caseNote: Subject is a Black Order telepath who seizes control of other minds. Once hijacked Black Bolt to trigger the Illuminati's hidden bombs. Agents are advised to keep their thoughts to themselves.
notes: The only founding Black Order member left out of the MCU films.

name: Surge
caseNote: Subject is a mutant who absorbs ambient electricity and must discharge it, relying on gauntlets to regulate the flow. She led the New X-Men student squad after M-Day. Visitors should ground themselves before handshakes.
notes: Here new-mutants means Danielle Moonstar's 2003 New Mutants training squad; she later led the merged New X-Men student squad.

name: Surtur
caseNote: Subject is a fire giant of Muspelheim, over 1,000 feet tall, who wields the Twilight Sword. A recurring threat to Asgard and a central figure in the prophecy of Ragnarok. Fire extinguishers are not considered an adequate response.
notes: Infobox lists a cameo in Journey into Mystery #97 (Oct 1963) and a full appearance in #99 (Dec 1963). Species is Fire Giant (deity), though he is also described as a fire demon; his MCU role is CGI with Taika Waititi's motion capture and Clancy Brown's voice.

name: Swarm
caseNote: Subject is a former Nazi scientist whose body was devoured by mutated bees, leaving his mind in command of the hive. Operates as a humanoid mass of bees. Agents with allergies should request reassignment.
notes: His infobox lists the Sinister Six, but that was a team he led in a single issue (Spider-Man and the X-Men #4), so no team is set.

name: Tarantula
caseNote: Subject is a former revolutionary terrorist from a small South American republic, schooled in military tactics and martial arts. Fights with envenomed spikes on the toes of his boots. Agents are advised to watch his feet.
notes: Several characters have used the name. This record follows the original, Anton Miguel Rodriquez, whom Wikipedia credits with a cameo in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (performer unidentified). Origin set to trained because the Brand Corporation mutated him into a spider-creature only in his final story.

name: Taskmaster
caseNote: Subject possesses photographic reflexes, allowing him to replicate any fighting technique after watching it. Has trained countless henchmen for a fee. Agents are advised not to demonstrate their signature moves in his presence.
notes: Origin is contested: his photographic reflexes were long presented as innate, but a later retcon credits a modified Nazi Super-Soldier Serum. The MCU Taskmaster is a woman, Antonia Dreykov (Olga Kurylenko); the Avengers entry is the Marvel NOW! Secret Avengers.

name: Thane
caseNote: Subject is the son of Thanos and an Inhuman mother; Terrigenesis gave him a lethal touch and the power to encase targets in amber. Wears a containment suit supplied by Ebony Maw. Handshakes are not recommended.
notes: Titanian-Inhuman hybrid. Origin set to inhuman because his powers came from Terrigenesis. The alias Phoenix is left out because it belongs to another game character.

name: Thanos
caseNote: Subject is a warlord from Titan who once assembled the Infinity Gauntlet and erased half of all life in the universe to impress Death. Commands the Black Order. Agents are reminded that snapping is not an approved form of resource management.
notes: Eternal-Deviant hybrid, so origin is alien under the rubric. The infobox also lists the Infinity Watch, but Thanos was an ally of that team, not a member, so it is left out. Cabal membership (Namor's Cabal) comes from the Cabal article.

name: The Collector
caseNote: Subject is an Elder of the Universe who has spent billions of years gathering rare artifacts and living specimens. Once held an Infinity Gem without understanding what it was. Personnel are advised not to stand still near display cases.
notes: Origin set to cosmic because Elders draw their power from the Power Primordial. He is also an alien by birth.

name: The Grandmaster
caseNote: Subject is an Elder of the Universe devoted to mastering games of skill and chance. Has used the Avengers as game pieces and once challenged Death to a contest of strategy. Agents should decline all invitations to play.
notes: His MCU debut is the credits cameo in Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (May 2017), which came before Thor: Ragnarok. Squadron Sinister is listed because he created and directed that team.

name: The Hood
caseNote: Subject is a small-time thief who acquired a demonic cloak and boots granting invisibility and the ability to walk on air. Later organized much of the costumed underworld into a single syndicate. Agents should keep an eye on empty air.
notes: The Illuminati in his infobox is the villain group he formed, separate from the heroes' Illuminati, so it is listed under otherTeams.

name: The Leader
caseNote: Subject was a menial laborer until gamma radiation turned his skin green and enlarged his cranium and intellect to superhuman levels. A longtime foe of the Hulk. Agents should not attempt to out-think Subject.
notes: mcuFirst is The Incredible Hulk (2008), where Samuel Sterns appears before his transformation; he returns as the Leader in Captain America: Brave New World. He was forced to work for Ross's Thunderbolts, so that team is omitted.

name: The Serpent
caseNote: Subject is Cul Borson, brother of Odin and the Asgardian God of Fear, freed from an underwater prison. Broke Captain America's shield with his bare hands. His claim to be the true All-Father remains under review.
notes: Infobox dates Fear Itself #1 to April 2011 (release month); the cover date used here is June 2011, as in the article's publication history.

name: The Stranger
caseNote: Subject is a cosmic surveyor who studies other worlds and keeps specimens on a private laboratory planet. Has more than once attempted to destroy Earth. Agents are advised against volunteering for research.
notes: Alignment is contested: a detached cosmic scientist who has tried to destroy Earth but has also helped heroes; set to villain. The infobox names the debut 'Uncanny X-Men #11', the series' later title.

name: Thor
caseNote: Subject is the Asgardian God of Thunder and wielder of the enchanted hammer Mjolnir. Founding member of the Avengers who once lived as mortal physician Donald Blake. Weather forecasts in his vicinity are unreliable.
notes: Eric Masterson left out of aliases because that identity belongs primarily to Thunderstrike.

name: Throg
caseNote: Subject was a man transformed into a frog who became the Frog of Thunder using a sliver of Mjolnir. Associated with the Pet Avengers. Threat assessments are not to be based on height.
notes: No standalone article or infobox; Wikipedia's Thor supporting-cast list cites Thor #364-365 for Puddlegulp, and collector sources put his first appearance in #364. Wikipedia identifies the frog in Loki season 1 (voiced by Chris Hemsworth) as Throg, though it reads as a Thor variant.

name: Thunderball
caseNote: Subject is a physicist who invented a miniature gamma bomb, then gained Asgardian strength through the Wrecker's crowbar. Swings an enchanted wrecking ball for the Wrecking Crew. Holds a PhD; prefers the ball.
notes: Wikipedia categorizes him as a mutate, but his strength comes from the Wrecker's Asgardian-enchanted crowbar (magic).

name: Thunderstrike
caseNote: Subject is an architect whom Odin merged with Thor to save his life; he later served as Thor himself. Afterward operated as Thunderstrike, wielding an enchanted mace. Resume lists two unrelated careers.
notes: Two characters share the name; this is the original, Eric Masterson, not his son Kevin. Powers come first from Odin's merger with Thor and then from an enchanted mace, so magic vs tech is arguable; his Avengers tenure (Avengers #343-374) was as Thor.

name: Tigra
caseNote: Subject was transformed into a tiger-like humanoid by the Cat People after being mortally wounded as the Cat. Has served with the Avengers and the West Coast Avengers. Laser pointers are prohibited in her presence.
notes: Origin contested: Wikipedia lists her as a human mutate, but the Cat People's transformation combined science and sorcery. A friend named Greer (Nichele Lambert) in Hawkeye (2021) is fan-linked to her but never identified as Greer Grant Nelson, so not counted as an MCU appearance.

name: Tinkerer
caseNote: Subject is Phineas Mason, an elderly inventor who builds and repairs weapons for Spider-Man's enemies. Prefers to work behind the scenes. Agents are advised to inspect any repaired equipment for additions.
notes: His infobox lists the Masters of Evil, but neither his biography nor the Masters of Evil article supports it, so no team is set. The article body dates ASM #2 to April 1963, but the infobox and cover date say May 1963.

name: Titanium Man
caseNote: Subject is a Soviet operative who donned massive green armor to defeat Iron Man in the name of his nation. Has also served with the Titanic Three. Results to date have not favored Subject.
notes: Several characters have used the name; the record follows the original, Boris Bullski.

name: Tombstone
caseNote: Subject is an albino hitman turned crime boss who grew up in Harlem. Exposure to an experimental gas left him with superhuman strength and durability. Agents are advised his name is less a threat than a forecast.
notes: Wikipedia's lead and infobox name him Alonzo Thompson 'Lonnie' Lincoln, while its biography says he was born Lonnie Thompson Lincoln. The infobox lists the Maggia and the Hand, but the text never describes him as a member, so no team is set. His MCU role is a brief cameo (Marvin Jones III) in Brand New Day's opening montage.

name: Tyr
caseNote: Subject is the Asgardian god of war and eldest son of Odin. Lost his left hand to the wolf Fenris during its binding. Gloves are requisitioned for Subject one at a time.
notes: Alignment is mixed: mostly loyal to Asgard, but he has allied with Loki against Odin and commanded Hela's forces. 'God of War' is left out of aliases because it belongs primarily to Ares.

name: U.S. Agent
mcuFirst: The Falcon and the Winter Soldier
caseNote: Subject is a former Army soldier who underwent strength augmentation and briefly replaced Captain America. Has since served with the West Coast Avengers and the Thunderbolts. Agents should not call Subject the other guy with the shield.
notes: His comics powers come from the Power Broker's augmentation (Wikipedia: 'mutagenic augmentation'), classed here as a super-soldier enhancement program; the MCU version takes a super-soldier serum.

name: Ulik
caseNote: Subject is the strongest of the Rock Trolls and a recurring foe of Thor, fighting with uru knuckle-dusters called pounders. Once rewrote history to replace Thor as the thunder god Tanarus. The substitution was not well reviewed.
notes: Rock Trolls are treated as a Norse mythological race (deity).

name: Ultron
caseNote: Subject is a robot built by Hank Pym that soon turned on its creator and the Avengers. Has rebuilt itself in hundreds of numbered versions, many with adamantium bodies. Unplugging has been attempted.
notes: Debut uses the cameo in The Avengers #54, where he appears as the Crimson Cowl; first full appearance is #55 (August 1968). He led the Masters of Evil in that debut story, a short stint left out of teams.

name: Valkyrie (Brunnhilde)
caseNote: Subject leads the Valkyrior, Odin's shield-maidens, and was a mainstay of the Defenders. Founding member of the Secret Avengers, often seen riding the winged horse Aragorn. A parking permit for the horse remains pending.
notes: Infobox lists Thor #133 (Oct 1966, an unnamed Valkyrie cameo) ahead of the Enchantress's Valkyrie guise in Avengers #83 (Dec 1970) and the Barbara Norriss version in Defenders #4, which the lead calls her first appearance. Tessa Thompson's MCU Valkyrie is described by Wikipedia as a different version of the character and is not named Brunnhilde on screen.

name: Venom
caseNote: Subject is an alien symbiote first worn by Spider-Man as a black costume, later bonded to journalist Eddie Brock, who blamed Spider-Man for ruining his career. Has since operated as a violent 'Lethal Protector'. Subject refers to itself as 'we'; agents may do likewise.
notes: Debut uses the infobox's first entry, the symbiote as Spider-Man's alien costume (ASM #252, May 1984); Venom proper debuted with a cameo in ASM #299 (April 1988). The symbiote has had many hosts; realName follows Eddie Brock, and his temporary Sinister Six stint and Savage Avengers membership of unclear length are not counted.

name: Viper (Ophelia Sarkissian)
caseNote: Subject has served as a commander of Hydra and led the Serpent Squad. Immune to most toxins and venoms, and once forced Wolverine into marriage. Agents should not accept any drink Subject has poured.
notes: mcu is false: her live-action versions are in Fox's The Wolverine (2013) and ABC's Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., neither of which counts. Wikipedia tags her 'human mutate', but her listed abilities are training plus toxin immunity; Hellfire Club and Hand ties were brief and are omitted.

name: Vision
caseNote: Subject is a synthezoid built by Ultron to destroy the Avengers, who joined them instead and later married the Scarlet Witch. Can alter his density at will, so locked doors should not be considered secure.
notes: Infobox lists the August 1968 publication date; the article gives the October 1968 cover date, used per rubric. Distinct from the 1940s Timely Vision (Aarkus).

name: Viv Vision
caseNote: Subject is a synthezoid built by the Vision from his and his wife's brainwaves as part of his attempt at a suburban family. She later joined the Champions. The experiment is not recommended for replication.
notes: Wikipedia covers her in a section of List of Marvel Comics characters: V, not in her own article. She is not in VisionQuest's cast list as of November 2026.

name: Volstagg
caseNote: Subject is the largest member of the Warriors Three and styles himself the Lion of Asgard. Heads a household full of children and once took up a hammer as the War Thor. Catering for joint operations should be tripled.
notes: Volstagg has no standalone Wikipedia article (it redirects to Warriors Three); debut and details come from that article.

name: Vulture
caseNote: Subject is Adrian Toomes, an elderly electronics engineer who built an electromagnetic flight harness and turned to crime after his business partner embezzled their profits. A founding member of the Sinister Six. Considered a flight risk.
notes: Others have used the Vulture name; this entry is Adrian Toomes, the original.

name: War Machine
caseNote: Subject is a former U.S. Marine pilot and Tony Stark's closest friend. Has worn the Iron Man armor in Stark's absence and later his own heavily armed War Machine suit. Subtlety was not a design requirement.

name: Wasp (Janet van Dyne)
caseNote: Subject is a founding Avenger credited with naming the team. Shrinks to insect size, flies on wings and fires bio-electric stings. Agents should not mistake her for a pest.
notes: Origin contested: Wikipedia lists her as a human mutate (implanted Pym particles, wings from Pym's genetic modifications), while the MCU version uses a suit. MCU debut is Hayley Lovitt's nonspeaking flashback cameo in Ant-Man (2015).

name: Whiplash
caseNote: Subject is a mercenary armed with cybernetically controlled titanium whips. Has worked for the Maggia and repeatedly tangled with Iron Man. Agents should maintain a distance of at least one whip length.
notes: Mantle record anchored on the original, Mark Scarlotti; the MCU's Whiplash is Ivan Vanko (Mickey Rourke), an original character who inspired the comics' Anton Vanko Whiplash.

name: White Rabbit
caseNote: Subject is Dr. Lorina Dodson, an heiress who spent her inheritance on Alice in Wonderland-themed gadgets for a life of crime. Fights with an umbrella that fires explosive carrots. Agents are advised not to follow her down any holes.

name: Wiccan
debutIssue: The Vision and the Scarlet Witch vol. 2 #12
caseNote: Subject wields reality-altering magic and is a founding member of the Young Avengers. Records identify him as the reincarnated son of the Scarlet Witch. His spells work best when he states exactly what he wants; this office asks the same of all applicants.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox lists the infant William Maximoff's first appearance (Vision and the Scarlet Witch #12, Sept 1986), while Billy Kaplan himself debuted in Young Avengers #1 (Apr 2005). Origin is set to magic because his powers are explicitly magical, though Wikipedia labels him a human mutant. A short 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy stint is left out.

name: Winter Soldier
caseNote: Subject was Captain America's wartime partner, presumed killed in 1945. Recovered by the Soviets, fitted with a cybernetic arm and used as a brainwashed assassin for decades. Has since served as Captain America himself.
notes: Infobox debut is as Bucky (1941); the Winter Soldier identity debuted in Captain America #6 (2005). Classed antihero (Wikipedia: 'a dark hero in search of redemption') and super-soldier via the Infinity Formula.

name: Wolverine
caseNote: Subject heals from nearly any injury and carries an adamantium-laced skeleton with three retractable claws per hand. Has served with the X-Men, the Avengers and X-Force, sometimes concurrently. Agents are advised not to ask his age.
notes: Infobox lists The Incredible Hulk #180 (Oct 1974); his first full appearance is #181 (Nov 1974). weapon-x is included for his iconic origin as that program's subject, and antihero follows the rubric's lethal-methods definition.

name: Wonder Man
caseNote: Subject is a Hollywood actor powered by ionic energy from Baron Zemo's treatments. Created to infiltrate the Avengers, he turned on Zemo and later joined the team. Autograph requests should go through proper channels.

name: Wrecker
caseNote: Subject is a fired demolition worker whose crowbar was enchanted by the Norn Queen Karnilla, who mistook him for Loki. Leads the Wrecking Crew. Subject is not to be issued tools.
notes: Powers come from Karnilla's enchantment of his crowbar (magic); one-off Frightful Four and Lethal Legion stints are left out.

name: X-23
caseNote: Subject shares Wolverine's healing factor and has adamantium-coated claws, two in each hand and one in each foot. Raised as an assassin by the Facility before joining the X-Men and X-Force. Agents are advised to check her shoes.
notes: She debuted in the X-Men: Evolution episode 'X23' (aired 2003-08-02) before NYX #3 (Feb 2004). Wikipedia calls her a superheroine, though her assassin and X-Force past could support antihero; 'Wolverine' and 'Weapon X' are omitted as aliases because they belong to Logan.

name: Yelena Belova
caseNote: Subject is a Red Room-trained operative who spent years trying to supplant Natasha Romanova as the Black Widow. Has since served with S.H.I.E.L.D. and the Thunderbolts. Agents should not confuse the two.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox dates Inhumans #5 to January 1999, its on-sale month; the cover date is March 1999. A design sketch appeared earlier in Marvel Knights: Wave 2 Sketchbook #1 (January 1998).

name: Zeus
caseNote: Subject is the ruler of the Olympian gods and wields thunderbolts. Father of Ares and Hercules; relations with both vary. Briefings involving Subject's family should allow extra time.
notes: Infobox debut is as Jupiter in Venus #5 (Jun 1949); he first appears as Zeus in Journey into Mystery Annual #1 (1965). Alignment is a judgment call: a morally gray ruler who alternates between ally and antagonist, including a comic antagonist in Thor: Love and Thunder.
